analysis.one_liner: Taxes household wealth above $50 million, rising to 3% on billion-dollar fortunes.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 25, 2026 with 50 cosponsors, all Democrats, and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, where it has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new annual tax on the net worth — total assets minus debts — of the wealthiest households. Households worth over $50 million would pay 2% a year on their wealth above that line, and anything over $1 billion would be taxed at 3%. The bill also adds $100 billion in IRS funding over ten years and requires the IRS to audit at least 30% of wealth-tax payers each year. It has been referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit to the extent the new revenue reduces deficits or funds public services — the bill's revenue is not earmarked for any specific program, though it does fund IRS enforcement and taxpayer services directly. If Congress later passes a universal health insurance program that bans duplicate private coverage, the rate on billion-dollar fortunes doubles to 6%, linking the tax to a Medicare-for-All-style expansion.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an annual 2% tax on each household's net worth above $50 million and 3% above $1 billion, levied on all property wherever located, minus debts owed.
Doubles the top rate to 6% in any year in which a universal health insurance program covering all residents is in effect, tying the wealth tax to a potential Medicare-for-All-style program.
Authorizes $100 billion in IRS appropriations for fiscal 2027–2037: $70 billion for enforcement, $10 billion for taxpayer services, and $20 billion for business systems modernization.
Requires the IRS to audit at least 30% of wealth-tax payers every year, and adds tougher penalties for large valuation understatements, including a 50% penalty for gross valuation misstatements.
Strengthens disclosure rules to reach assets parked in foreign corporations, partnerships, or trusts, and directs the Treasury to leverage existing foreign-account data for enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: The roughly 0.1% of households with net worth above $50 million, who would pay the new annual tax on top of existing income, capital gains, and estate taxes. Married couples are treated as one taxpayer, and the tax also applies to certain trusts and to covered expatriates renouncing citizenship, who face a 40% rate on their way out.

drawbacks.text: Valuing assets is genuinely hard: the bill requires Treasury to invent new valuation methods for assets that are not publicly traded and lack an easily determined value, including formula-based estimates and retrospective adjustments, which will produce disputes and litigation.

The bill itself acknowledges cash-flow problems: it lets the Treasury grant up to 5-year payment extensions to taxpayers with severe liquidity constraints or hardship to ongoing enterprises — a sign that an annual tax on illiquid wealth (like private company stakes) can be hard to pay without selling assets.

Avoidance pressure is built into the design: the bill imposes a 40% rate on covered expatriates and requires anti-avoidance reporting rules, measures responding to the risk that very wealthy people shift assets abroad or renounce citizenship.
The revenue is not committed to any specific public benefit; the bill raises money without earmarking it, so its practical effect on ordinary people depends on later spending decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: a tax aimed squarely at the very top of the wealth distribution, with aggressive enforcement and audit requirements built in. The main risks are administrative and practical rather than distributional — valuing private assets is hard, some taxpayers will contest valuations for years, and the bill leaves the revenue uncommitted. On its face, the costs fall almost entirely on households that hold the most wealth.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and has had no further action; the Congress is still in session, so it could still move, but nothing is scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act of 2026 in the House on March 25, 2026.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the public action history shows no markup, hearing, or vote since.
The bill has 49 cosponsors in addition to the sponsor — all Democrats, none Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost — the bill is simply sitting in committee. If it stays there, the households it would tax are better off, since a wealth tax above $50 million would otherwise fall on them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Too early to say; no action yet

sides.party_line_note: All 50 supporters (sponsor plus 49 cosponsors) are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the committee controlled by the House Republican majority has not acted on the bill.

industries.note: Households worth over $50 million would owe a new annual tax of 2% on wealth above that line and 3% above $1 billion, regardless of income. This is the bill's central cost, falling on roughly the top tenth of one percent of households.

industries.industry: Private wealth management, trust, and tax advisory firms
industries.note: Ultra-high-net-worth clients would need annual asset valuations, compliance work, and possibly restructuring, generating fee income — but the underlying tax shrinks the fortunes that fee income depends on. Firms that help clients shelter assets abroad would face new reporting rules aimed at exactly that practice.

The bill does not establish single-payer health care itself, but it doubles the wealth tax rate to 6% if Congress enacts a universal health program that bans duplicate private coverage — a deterrent structure that private insurers would want to avoid, since it raises the price of Medicare-for-All-style legislation.
The bill authorizes $100 billion over a decade for enforcement, taxpayer services, and modernization, reversing years of funding pressure on the agency that administers the tax code for everyone.

analysis.trajectory: Versions of this wealth tax introduced in earlier Congresses never received a committee markup, and the odds are worse now: Republicans hold 223 House seats and chair Ways and Means, and the committee has taken no action since referral. The realistic path is that the bill sits in committee until this Congress ends, with the Democratic cosponsor list potentially growing but the bill never reaching the floor.
